output.brief: The drop in first-year enrolment came from lower yield, meaning fewer admitted students chose to enrol. It did not come from a weaker applicant pool: applications and admits both rose. The strongest pattern is by scholarship tier. Award amounts were cut in the Dean's tier ($14,000 to $9,000) and the Merit tier ($9,000 to $5,000). Yield fell about 13 points in each. Yield in the Presidential tier and the no-award group barely moved. That rules out a general softening in demand. The portal delay does not explain it well. Early-action students got decisions and awards on the old timetable, and their yield fell by about as much (45.2% to 37.8%) as regular decision's (39.0% to 31.5%). The slow regular-decision turnaround was real, and it probably cost some individual students. But it is not the main driver. I'm fairly confident, though not certain. The tier data doesn't split early action from regular decision, and I haven't checked competitor pricing or the student survey. Replacing the Director would punish the wrong party and leave the cause in place. Next steps: take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee with a costed proposal to restore awards in the tiers where yield fell, before award letters go out. Also set a regular-decision turnaround target. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the missing-transcript claims are checked.
